ANP is released when there is high blood pressure and acts on the kidneys to decrease NaCl reabsorption in the DCT and Collecting duct. It also increases K+ and H+ secretion in the DCT and collecting duct. This leads to water reabsorption being decreased as the osmotic potential of the tubular fluid increases. This increases urine output and reduces blood volume.  Aldosterone is released in response to low blood pressure and acts on the DCT and Collecting duct to increase NaCl reabsorption and water excretion. It also increases K+ secretion and H+ absorption which has the opposite effect. ADH is released in response to increased plasma osmolality and acts on the Collecting duct and Loop of Henle to increase water reabsorption.  Information is from Dr Johnson's lecture on Kidney Regulation. Angiotensin II increases blood pressure by vasoconstriction and increasing aldosterone to increase sodium reabsorption at the expense of potassium and water. This raises the blood volume and osmolarity which in turn increases the pressure. It also upregulates the thirst reflex as well as ADH. Renin is the enzyme used to convert angiotensin I into II therefore it is not stimulated by angiotensin II but rather angiotensin-renin system (A.R.S) is activated when there is a decrease in the renal blood flow. This is reduced by hypotension or increased NaCl excretion. It is mainly released by juxtaglomerular cells. The angiotensinogen is converted into angiotensin I in the lung by the action of the renin. Angiotensin I is then converted into angiotensin II by the action of ACE (found in the lungs and kidneys). This has a positive feedback on the release of renin. Angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction which increases the blood pressure and therefore the renal blood flow. It also increases aldosterone to increase the reabsorption of sodium at the expense of potassium and water. This leads to an increase in the plasma volume and osmolarity which further increases the blood pressure. Angiotensin II also upregulates the thirst mechanism and ADH. ADH increases the amount of water reabsorbed from the collecting ducts. This again increases the volume of the blood. Non steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are a class of medications that are used to relieve pain and inflammation. Common NSAIDs include ibuprofen and naproxen sodium. Aspirin also belongs to this drug class, but it has an added effect as an antiplatelet drug. All NSAIDs inhibit both the enzyme cyclooxygenase (COX) 1 and COX 2. Cyclooxygenase converts arachidonic acid into biologically active molecules called prostaglandins. Prostaglandins induce inflammation by causing vasodilation and increasing the sensitivity of nociceptive neurons. They also stimulate the release of histamine from mast cells and other chemical mediators of inflammation. By inhibiting the activity of the COX enzyme, NSAIDs prevent the formation of prostaglandins. This reduces inflammation, relieving symptoms associated with many types of chronic conditions. NSAIDs may be taken on an empty or full stomach. However, taking them after eating may help decrease the risk of gastrointestinal side effects such as bleeding and ulcers. If NSAIDs are taken regularly, they should always be taken after eating to further minimize these side effects. Taking NSAIDs with food does not appear to affect their absorption. NSAIDs may interact with many different medications. For example, antacids containing calcium or aluminum can decrease the absorption of NSAIDs. Pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardium (the lining around the heart). It can be caused by infection (typically viral), injury to the chest wall, cancer, other diseases, medications, or unknown reasons. Symptoms include chest pain that gets worse when lying down, shortness of breath, swelling in your legs or belly. Complications include congestive heart failure and sudden death. Diagnosis is usually based on symptoms and physical examination. An echocardiogram may help confirm the diagnosis.Treatment depends on the type of pericarditis and how severe it is. Antibiotics and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may be used for bacterial or tuberculous pericarditis. Corticosteroids are often used for idiopathic (of unknown cause) or viral pericarditis. Treating the underlying cause may also help. If pericarditis causes too much fluid to build up, a needle or surgery may be needed to remove some of the fluid from around the heart.Pericarditis is typically acute, but can become chronic if left untreated. In most cases, pericarditis resolves without complication within several weeks to several months. Glenoid labrum is a fibrocartilaginous structure that surrounds the glenoid fossa of the scapula and functions as a joint between the scapula and humerus. It consists of three parts - the superior, middle, and inferior glenohumeral ligaments. The superior glenohumeral ligament attaches to the inferior aspect of the greater tuberosity of the humerus and inserts into the anterior and posterior bands of the glenoid labrum. The middle glenohumeral ligament is a thick band that originates from the posterior surface of the proximal humerus and inserts into the anterior and posterior bands of the glenoid labrum. The inferior glenohumeral ligament is a thin band that attaches to the inferior aspect of the greater tuberosity of the humerus and inserts into the anterior band of the glenoid labrum.
